opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That project, History Flow, which I did with Fernanda Viégas back around 2003, really changed how I thought about what visualization is *for*.

At the time, Wikipedia was still pretty new, and there was a lot of skepticism. People asked how it could possibly work if anyone could edit anything. Wouldn't vandals just destroy it? Those were empirical questions, but nobody had a good way to look at the data. The edit histories were all public, but they were just long lists of revisions. You couldn't see the shape of what was happening.

So we built a fairly simple visualization. Each version of an article was a vertical line, and the text was colored by who contributed it, so you could watch pieces of text persist, move around, or disappear over time. The moment we started looking at real articles, patterns jumped out that we hadn't expected. You could see edit wars as this zigzag pattern where two versions alternated back and forth. And you could see vandalism, like someone deleting an entire page, as a sudden black gap. What surprised us was how *short* those gaps often were. Mass deletions were frequently repaired within a few minutes. That was a real finding about how the community worked, and it came straight out of looking at pictures.

What I took away was that visualization isn't just a way to present results you already have. It can be an instrument for discovery, a bit like a microscope. You point it at something complicated, and it shows you structure you didn't know to ask about. You often don't know your hypothesis in advance. The picture suggests the hypothesis, and then you can go back and test it more rigorously.

That idea has stayed with me ever since, including in my more recent work on understanding neural networks. A neural network is another big, opaque system full of structure we don't understand yet. The instinct is the same: find a way to see inside it, and let what you see guide the questions you ask.

r001.rationale: The response says revision histories were only long lists, making it hard to see what was happening, and that visualizing them revealed patterns such as edit wars and quickly repaired deletions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that project—History Flow, which I did with Fernanda Viégas back around 2003—really started almost as a curiosity. Wikipedia was still young, and a lot of people, frankly, assumed it couldn't work. Anyone can edit anything? It should have been chaos. So we wanted to just look at what was actually happening to the text over time.

And what we found was that the picture was very different from the intuition. You'd see vandalism, sure—someone would wipe out an entire article—but then in the visualization it would show up as this tiny sliver, because it got reverted within minutes. The stability of the thing was much more visible than the chaos. And you'd also see these beautiful patterns: long stretches where articles grew in a kind of sedimentary way, contributors adding layers, and occasional bursts of controversy where the text would thrash back and forth, which we started calling edit wars.

The lesson I took from that was that visualization isn't just a way to present a result you already know. It's a way to discover things you didn't know to ask about. We hadn't set out to find that vandalism got reverted in a median of a couple of minutes—we saw the shape first, and then we went and measured it. The picture generated the hypothesis. That's a different mode of research than starting from a question and designing an experiment.

The other thing it taught me is that visualizing a system changes how people relate to it. Once Wikipedians saw History Flow, some of them started using it—or ideas like it—to understand their own community. The tool became a kind of mirror. And that stuck with me, because later, when I started working on neural networks, I realized the situation was almost the same: here's a system that's producing all this behavior, nobody fully understands why, and the first step is just to look at it honestly and let it surprise you.

r001.rationale: The response describes patterns revealed by History Flow, including quickly reverted vandalism and edit wars, but does not say these patterns were difficult to discern by manually browsing article revisions.

astra-6.text:
One of the things that struck me was that the history of a Wikipedia article could be much more revealing than the article itself. You see this apparently coherent piece of text, but behind it there might be a tremendous amount of negotiation—people adding things, removing things, putting them back.

Fernanda Viégas and I worked on a visualization called History Flow that let us see those patterns over time. Some of the most interesting moments were the disruptions: somebody would delete almost everything, and then someone else would restore it. Or you’d see a section persist while the text around it kept changing. Those patterns raised questions about how collaboration actually worked.

That helped convince me that visualization wasn’t just a way to present a result you already understood. It could be a way to discover what questions to ask. You’d notice a pattern, go back and read the edits, and try to understand what had happened. The picture didn’t explain people’s motivations by itself, but it gave us a way into a process that would otherwise have been very difficult to see.

r001.rationale: The response describes History Flow revealing patterns in article edits over time and says the process would otherwise have been very difficult to see. It also explains that the visualization helped identify patterns before returning to read the edits.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the things that struck me was that an article looks like a finished object, but underneath it is this ongoing social process. When Fernanda Viégas and I visualized the edit histories, you could see passages appear, disappear, and come back. An argument between editors could leave a very recognizable visual pattern.

That changed how I thought about visualization. It wasn’t simply a way to present an answer once you’d done the research. It could be a way to discover what questions to ask. You’d notice a pattern, go back to the edits, and try to understand what people were doing. The picture didn’t explain their motivations by itself, but it gave you a place to start investigating.

r001.rationale: The response says the visualization made edit patterns visible, but does not state that those patterns were difficult to discern by manually browsing revisions.
